newsitem.title: SPAIN: Bank of Spain withholds rate cut despite tame CPI.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Spain withholds rate cut despite tame CPI.

text.p: The Bank of Spain left its key interest rate steady on Friday and economists predicted it would wait to see the government's 1997 budget draft before easing rates, despite surprisingly tame inflation in August.
Spanish consumer prices rose 0.3 percent in August over July, for an unchanged inflation rate of 3.7 percent year-on-year.

Economists had forecast an August rise of 0.5 percent and a year-on-year rate of 3.9 percent, pushed higher by an emergency tax increase on alcohol and tobacco imposed to fund a gap in the former government's 1995 budget.

Just before the data's release, the central bank decided to hold its key money market rate steady at 7.25 percent. The Bank of Spain has lowered its rates five times this year from nine percent in early January.

"I don't think this will be a key figure for the Bank of Spain. The Bank is more worried about the budget, and that will be the subject that pushes them to move on rates," said Gregorio Gomez, economist at a Spanish brokerage.
The four-month-old conservative Popular Party administration must present a draft 1997 budget to parliament by the end of the month and cabinet approval is expected on September 27.

It has pledged to put forward an austere package that will secure Spain's participation in the launch of the European single currency in 1999. But it has so far given scant detail on how it will accomplish the task.
Like many of its European partners, one of Spain's toughest hurdles is narrowing its budget deficit to comply with single currency target of a three percent ratio to gross domestic product.
The government has pledged to reduce its deficit to the three percent threshhold next year from a projected 4.4 percent this year after around 6.6 percent in 1995.
"The Bank of Spain is more focused on the budget. Now they are pressuring the government to prepare an authentically restrictive budget," said Isabel Lasheras, economist at Societe Generale in Spain.
In an interview with a financial daily published on Friday, Treasury director Jaime Caruana said he expected Spain to meet the deficit criterion.
But it might not meet the debt criterion of 60 percent to GDP although there would be improvement next year.
Economists said they expected continued improvement in inflation this year.
"This is a good number, better than forecast. A positive surprise," said Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch. "Inflation will continue to decline in what is left of the year."
